nameStory: Field maple gets its straightforward name from its preferred habitat - open fields, farmland edges, and countryside areas rather than deep forests. Unlike its forest-dwelling cousins, this European native thrives in agricultural landscapes and has been planted along field boundaries for centuries. The name perfectly captures where you're most likely to spot this adaptable tree.
description: Field maple is a small to medium-sized deciduous tree that typically grows 25-35 feet tall with a rounded, compact crown. It's actually native to Europe but has been planted in New England as an ornamental and shade tree. The tree has a neat, tidy appearance with distinctive small maple leaves and produces the classic helicopter-seed pods that all maples are known for. It's much smaller than our native sugar maples and has a more refined, garden-friendly size.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small maple leaves, only 2-4 inches across, with 3-5 rounded lobes that feel thick and leathery to the touch. The lobes are much more rounded and blunt than other maples, and the leaves turn brilliant golden-yellow to orange-red in fall.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Develops distinctive corky ridges or wings on young branches and twigs that you can feel with your fingers - these raised, bark-like strips are unique among New England maples. Mature bark becomes gray-brown and furrowed.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Compact, rounded tree that stays relatively small compared to other maples, with dense branching that creates good shade. Often has multiple trunks or low branching, giving it a shrub-like appearance when young.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces typical maple 'helicopter' seeds (samaras) but they're smaller than sugar maple seeds and the wings spread almost horizontally, creating a nearly straight line across.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, greenish-yellow flowers appear in spring in small clusters, not particularly showy but they attract bees and other pollinators with their sweet scent.

habitat: In New England, field maple is primarily found in cultivated landscapes - parks, residential areas, college campuses, and as street trees. It prefers well-drained soils and full sun to partial shade, thriving in urban and suburban environments where it's been intentionally planted. You won't typically find it in natural forest settings, but rather in designed landscapes where it was chosen for its manageable size and attractive fall color.

seasonality.spring: Small clusters of greenish-yellow flowers appear before or with the emerging leaves, creating a subtle but sweet-scented display that attracts early pollinators.
seasonality.summer: Dense, rounded crown provides good shade with its thick, leathery leaves that stay green through hot weather. The corky bark ridges on twigs are most noticeable during leafy season.
seasonality.fall: Puts on a spectacular show with leaves turning bright golden-yellow to orange-red, often more vibrant than many native maples. Seeds ripen and helicopter down in late summer to early fall.
seasonality.winter: Bare tree shows its compact, rounded branching structure and the distinctive corky ridges on younger branches become a key identification feature.

funFact: Field maple bark was traditionally used to make a yellow dye, and in some parts of Europe, the sap was actually tapped like sugar maple to make a sweet syrup - though you'd need about twice as much sap to get the same amount of sugar!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with young Norway maples, but field maple's leaves are much smaller, thicker, and have rounded lobes rather than pointed ones. Remember: field maple leaves fit in your palm comfortably, while Norway maple leaves are dinner-plate sized. The corky wing ridges on field maple twigs are also a dead giveaway.
contextualKnowledge: Field maple is not native to New England but has been widely planted as an ornamental tree since colonial times. While it's not invasive like Norway maple, it's not contributing to native ecosystems either - it's essentially a well-behaved garden tree that stays where it's planted.
compareHints: Field maple is much smaller than sugar maple, red maple, or Norway maple, with distinctively small, thick, round-lobed leaves that set it apart from all other maples in New England. The corky bark ridges on twigs are unique among our regional maples. While Japanese maples can be similarly small, they have much more deeply cut, delicate leaves compared to field maple's simple, rounded lobes.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Red maple differs from sugar maple by its toothed leaf margins, red leaf stems, and earlier seed drop.
Unlike its maple relatives, striped maple has the distinctive white-striped bark that no other North American maple possesses.
Among New England's maples, sugar maples have the smoothest leaf edges (no teeth) and the most rounded lobe shapes, while red maples have serrated edges and more pointed lobes.
Norway maple differs from sugar maple by its milky leaf sap, earlier and more chartreuse spring flowers, and wider-angled seed wings.
Box elder stands out dramatically from other New England maples because it's the only one with compound leaves instead of the classic lobed maple leaf shape.
Among New England's maples, mountain maple is the odd one out—it's the only one that stays truly shrubby and forms colonies rather than growing into a single-trunked tree.

Among New England maples, silver maple stands out for its deeply dissected leaves and silvery undersides - much more dramatic than the shallow lobes of red maple or the more rounded lobes of sugar maple.
Among New England maples, sycamore maple stands out for its exceptionally large leaves on long stalks and drooping flower clusters.
Among New England maples, Amur maple is unique for its consistently small size and three-lobed leaves with the distinctly elongated center lobe.

Japanese maple differs from all native New England maples by having much more deeply divided, delicate leaves with 5-9 narrow lobes compared to the broader, less-divided leaves of sugar maple, red maple, and silver maple.
